Ten Human Fluencies, specified unit by unit.

Human Fluency is the second series beside Future Fluency. It opens through the same gate. Every learning outcome and every assessment criterion is on this page, in full, with the level check that holds each unit against the Ofqual Level 3 descriptor.

Section 1

What Human Fluency is

Future Fluency is about working well alongside AI. Human Fluency is about what stays yours: the things AI cannot do for you because it has no life to live. A body, something at stake, being answerable, caring about someone, wanting something, making meaning.

  • At Level 3 the learner applies each unit to their own work and life. Their own life is the evidence, not a case study.
  • Leading other people through any of this belongs to higher levels, and every unit's boundary says so.

The gate. Growth Mindset and Emotional Intelligence open both series. ZFF-GM-03 is specified on the Level 3 page. ZFF-EI-03 is new, and is specified here so that both series can use it.

The bridge. ZFF-CH-03, facing change in own working life, is the first unit of Future Fluency's Change Fluency. It is the pilot, and it links the two series.

Short units. Each unit is 12 to 15 hours, so it can be taken on its own. Every unit is built around one moment where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. The design note in each unit names the criterion that carries it.

Section 2

Structure and size

Credit is shown at the Ofqual convention of 1 credit per 10 hours of Total Qualification Time. Guided learning is shown as indicative, at half the TQT rounded up.

Section 3

The units

The gate
ZFF-EI-03

Understanding and Managing Emotions in Own Work and Life

Level3TQT15 hoursCredits1.5GLH8 indicativeFluencyThe gateCriteria15

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to notice, name and manage their own emotions in their own work and life, and to read the emotions of the people they deal with. Learners predict which emotions a week will bring, then log and name them several times a day. They find what sets their emotions off and how it shows. They select a way of managing an emotion, predict how it will go and try it. They check how well they read another person. They then review what worked and set the next step.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how emotionally intelligent they seem. Every criterion asks for a record, a description or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge maturity, calm or attitude. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. The learner chooses which events to log and use, and a situation can be described in general terms, so no criterion requires disclosing anything private. Learners can always reach a person for support. This unit shares the gate with ZFF-GM-03 and is open to both Future Fluency and Human Fluency learners.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to record and name own emotions across a week of own work and life.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record in writing a prediction of which emotions will come up most often in the coming week, and in which situations
1.2Keep a log at set points several times a day for at least five days, naming each emotion with the most precise word available
1.3Compare the log with the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the difference, with reference to research on naming emotions precisely
LO2
The learner will: Be able to identify what triggers own emotions and how they show in own behaviour.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify from the log at 1.2 the situations that most often came before a strong emotion
2.2Describe how two of those emotions showed in what the learner said or did at the time
2.3Describe how a person present at one of those events saw it, and how their view differs from the learner's
LO3
The learner will: Be able to select and use a strategy to manage an emotion in own work or life.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe two strategies for managing an emotion, such as rethinking the situation and putting the feeling into words, and when each is likely to help
3.2Select one strategy for a situation the learner expects to meet, and record in writing a prediction of how it will go
3.3Use the strategy in that situation, then compare the result with the prediction made at 3.2 and explain the difference
LO4
The learner will: Be able to interpret the emotions of another person in own work or life and adjust own response.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Interpret the emotion of another person in an interaction the learner took part in, giving the cues the interpretation rests on
4.2Check the interpretation against what the person later said or did, and record whether it was accurate
4.3Describe how the learner adjusted their own response as a result of the check
LO5
The learner will: Be able to review how own emotions have been managed and set the next step.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Evaluate which strategy worked best for the learner, and in which situations, using the records from LO1 and LO3
5.2Review how well own predictions at 1.1 and 3.2 matched what happened, and what that shows
5.3State the next step to be taken, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

5 learning outcomes, 15 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own emotions in own work and life, is defined. The situation at 3.3 is non-routine because the learner does not control how it unfolds. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 4.1 and 5.1. Aware of different perspectives: 2.3 and 4.2. Review effectiveness: LO5.

Boundary. The learner manages their own emotions and reads the people they deal with directly. Working with the emotions of a department's people through a change in their roles is ZFF-EI-05 at Level 5. ZHF-MB-03 tracks attention, body signals, sleep, movement, stillness and meaning. It does not assess naming, managing or reading emotions. Where a learner takes both units, one log cannot be submitted as evidence for both.

Evidence

A prediction and emotion log (1.1, 1.2), a trigger record (LO2), a strategy record (3.2, 3.3), an interpretation check (LO4) and a short review (LO5), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Mayer and Salovey 1997; Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight 2015; Barrett 2017; Killingsworth and Gilbert 2010; Gross 1998; Gross and John 2003; Lieberman et al. 2007; Brooks 2014. Checked 21 October 2026.

Purpose Fluency
ZHF-PU-03

Choosing Own Goals

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyPurposeCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to tell the goals they chose from the goals they were handed, and to set one aim of their own. Learners sort their recent goals. They predict what they return to when nobody asks them to, then track it for two weeks. They set one aim, plan for the first obstacle and take the first step. After a month they decide whether the aim is still theirs.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how purposeful they seem. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge commitment or motivation. Letting go of an aim at 4.2 meets the criterion as fully as keeping it. The wow moments sit at 2.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. No criterion requires disclosing anything private: the learner chooses which goals to use.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to judge which of own recent goals were chosen and which were handed to them.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select at least six goals from own work and life over the past year that differ in where they came from and in size, and justify the selection
1.2Judge each goal as chosen or handed, using a model of motivation from research, and explain any goal that does not fit either category cleanly
1.3Select one handed goal, describe how it looks to the person who set it, and evaluate which parts of their view the learner shares
LO2
The learner will: Be able to identify what they return to when nobody asks them to.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Record in writing a prediction of the activity the learner most often returns to without being asked, and the evidence from own life it is based on
2.2Keep a record over two weeks of freely chosen activities, with the time each took and how absorbed the learner was, and interpret the pattern it shows
2.3Compare the record with the prediction made at 2.1, and explain the difference
LO3
The learner will: Be able to set one aim of their own and take the first step.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Choose between at least two possible aims drawn from what was found at LO2, set the chosen aim with a date by which it will be reached, and justify the choice
3.2Identify the obstacles likely to get in the way, select the one most likely, and write an "if this happens, then I will" plan for it, explaining why that response was chosen
3.3Take the first step, compare what happened with the obstacle expected at 3.2, and explain any change made to the plan as a result
LO4
The learner will: Be able to review own aim and decide whether it is still own.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe progress towards the aim after at least four weeks, using records from the period
4.2Evaluate whether the aim still fits what matters to the learner, and decide to keep, change or let it go, giving reasons
4.3Review the goals selected at 1.1 in the light of the unit, and state the next step, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own goals, is defined. It is non-routine because the pattern at 2.2 is not known in advance, and the first step at 3.3 may meet an obstacle other than the one expected, so the plan has to be changed. Identify, select and use: 1.1, 3.1 and 3.2, where the learner chooses between options and justifies the choice. Interpret and evaluate: 1.2, 2.2, 2.3 and 4.2. Aware of different perspectives: 1.3. Review effectiveness: 3.3 and LO4. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 1.1 to 1.3 and 2.1 to 3.3 now ask for selection, justification or interpretation in place of listing, sorting, recording and setting, and the scope stays the learner's own goals.

Boundary. The learner chooses and pursues their own goals. Setting goals for other people or for a team is leadership and is outside this unit. ZHF-LD-03 compares the learner's values with their time and tests possible lives. This unit chooses, pursues and reviews one aim, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A goal sort (LO1), a prediction and activity record (2.1, 2.2), an aim with an "if, then" plan (3.1, 3.2), a first-step record (3.3) and a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Deci and Ryan 2000; Sheldon and Elliot 1999; Sheldon and Houser-Marko 2001; Ware 2012; Csikszentmihalyi 1990; Hill and Turiano 2014; Kamiya 1966; Locke and Latham 2002; Oettingen 2014; Gollwitzer and Sheeran 2006; Wrosch et al. 2003; Duke 2022. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-LD-03

Designing and Testing a Life

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyPurposeCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to look at the life they have and test a life they might want. Learners rank their values, predict where their time goes, then record it hour by hour. They rate their life across health, work, play and love. They test one possible life by talking to someone living it and trying a small piece. They then plan practice towards a real role and try the first session.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not whether their life is a good one. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge the learner's choices. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. Where a direction involves money, the unit gives skills and guidance only, never personal financial advice. The learner chooses what to record and share, so no criterion requires disclosing anything private. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare own values with where own time goes.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Rank the values that matter most to the learner, using a recognised list, and record a prediction of how a typical week's time divides across them
1.2Record own time hour by hour over at least three days, including one day away from work
1.3Compare the record with the ranking and the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the gap
LO2
The learner will: Be able to assess where own life is now across health, work, play and love.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Rate own life in each of the four areas, giving evidence for each rating
2.2Interpret the balance across the four areas, and identify the area that most needs attention, giving reasons
2.3Describe how a person who knows the learner well sees that balance, and where their view differs
LO3
The learner will: Be able to test a possible life through a small experiment.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe one possible direction for own life, and record in writing a prediction of how living it would feel
3.2Hold a conversation with a person already living that direction, and try one small piece of it, keeping a record
3.3Compare what was found with the prediction made at 3.1, and explain the difference, with reference to research on forecasting from another person's experience
LO4
The learner will: Be able to build and try a learning plan linked to a real role.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Select a real role linked to the direction tested at LO3, such as one in a job advert, and identify three skills it requires that the learner lacks
4.2Plan practice with feedback for each skill, stating who or what will give the feedback and when
4.3Carry out the first practice session, review how well the plan worked, and state the next step and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own life now and one possible direction, is defined. The experiment at LO3 is non-routine because its result is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.2 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 2.3 and 3.2. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner designs and tests their own life. Giving career guidance to others or designing roles for other people is outside this unit. ZHF-PU-03 chooses and pursues one aim. ZFF-GM-03 keeps the learner's skills current in their present role. This unit tests a direction the learner might move towards, so the three units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A values ranking and time record (LO1), a four-area rating (LO2), an experiment record (3.2, 3.3) and a learning plan with a practice log (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Schwartz 1992; Whillans, Weidman and Dunn 2016; Kahneman et al. 2004; Diener et al. 1985; Burnett and Evans 2016; Sirgy and Wu 2009; Winn 2014; Markus and Nurius 1986; Gilbert et al. 2009; Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer 1993; Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald 2014. Checked 21 October 2026.

Courage Fluency
ZHF-CO-03

Acting When Something Is at Risk

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyCourageCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to act for something that matters while the risk is real. Learners name what they avoid and what avoiding it costs. They predict how a feared conversation will go, have it and compare. They carry out one small act of courage in their own work and judge it. They raise a concern through a suitable channel and review what happened.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how brave they seem. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge confidence or character. The wow moment sits at 2.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. The learner chooses each act and its size, and a small one meets every criterion. No criterion requires a risk to the learner's safety, health or job, or disclosing anything private. A concern that is a safeguarding or legal matter goes through the employer's own procedure, and this unit does not replace it. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to identify what they avoid and what avoiding it costs.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Identify the things in own work or life that the learner avoids because of fear, or would regret not doing, and select the three that matter most, justifying the choice
1.2Describe what avoiding each will cost over the coming year, in time, opportunity or relationships
1.3Explain which of the three the learner is most likely to regret not doing, with reference to research on regret
LO2
The learner will: Be able to compare a forecast of a feared conversation or act with how it went.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select one feared conversation or act from own work or life, and record in writing a prediction of how it will go, including how the other person will react
2.2Carry it out, and record what happened, including how the other person responded
2.3Compare the result with the prediction made at 2.1, and explain the difference, with reference to research on how people misjudge others' reactions
LO3
The learner will: Be able to act on a value in own work when doing so carries a personal risk.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify a situation in own work where a value is at stake, and the personal risk of acting on it
3.2Choose between at least two possible small acts for that value, carry out the chosen act and record what was done, explaining why it was chosen
3.3Evaluate whether the act was courageous rather than reckless, against a stated definition of courage
LO4
The learner will: Be able to speak up about a concern in own work.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe a concern in own work and how it is likely to look to the person who would receive it, and select a suitable channel from those available, giving reasons
4.2Raise the concern through the channel selected at 4.1, and record what was said and the response
4.3Review how well raising the concern worked, comparing the response with what was expected at 4.1, and state what the learner would do differently next time

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one feared act and one concern in own work, is defined. The acts at 2.2, 3.2 and 4.2 are non-routine because the other person's response is not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 1.1, 2.1, 3.2 and 4.1, where the learner chooses what to act on, the act or the channel, and gives reasons. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 2.1, where the learner predicts the other person's reaction, and 4.1, where the learner sets out how the concern will look to the person who receives it. Review effectiveness: 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 1.1 and 3.2 now ask the learner to select and justify, and the double criterion at 4.3 was split, with the other person's view moved into 4.1 and 4.3 now a single review, so the count stays at 12.

Boundary. The learner acts with courage in their own work and life. Making it safe for a team to speak up is leadership and is outside this unit. ZHF-RE-03 is about recovering after a setback. This unit is about acting before the outcome is known, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

An avoidance list (LO1), a forecast and outcome record (LO2), an act record with its evaluation (LO3) and a concern record with a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Epley and Schroeder 2014; Bruk et al. 2018; Kardas, Kumar and Epley 2022; Gilovich and Medvec 1994, 1995; Hayes et al. 1996; Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson 1999; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Rate et al. 2007; Detert 2021; Darley and Latané 1968; Philpot et al. 2020; Milliken, Morrison and Hewlin 2003; Edmondson 1999. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-RE-03

Recovering From Setbacks

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyCourageCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to recover from setbacks in their own work and life. Learners find the pattern in how they explain their setbacks. They predict whether retelling one will change how it feels, then write about it and check. They build a recovery routine and use it for two weeks. They then test a claim about what a past hard time built in them against evidence.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how resilient they seem. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge strength or attitude. The wow moments sit at 2.3 and 4.2, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction or claim. The learner chooses which setbacks to use, a small one meets every criterion, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private. The unit is not therapy. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to identify the pattern in how they explain own setbacks.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe three setbacks from own work or life, and how the learner explained each at the time
1.2Sort each explanation as permanent or temporary, all-embracing or specific, and about self or about circumstances
1.3Interpret the pattern across the three, with reference to research on explanatory style
LO2
The learner will: Be able to retell a setback in more accurate terms.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Rate how threatening a recent setback feels, and record in writing a prediction of whether retelling it will change the rating
2.2Write about the setback in at least three short sessions, using own name and "you" in place of "I"
2.3Rate the setback again, compare the result with the prediction made at 2.1, and explain the difference
LO3
The learner will: Be able to build and use a recovery routine.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select recovery activities that include rest, time with people, learning something new and a choice the learner controls
3.2Use the routine for at least two weeks, keeping a record, including the days it was missed
3.3Evaluate which parts of the routine helped most, using the record
LO4
The learner will: Be able to describe what a past hard time built in them, and test the claim.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe a skill, relationship or habit the learner believes a past hard time built
4.2Test the claim against evidence from before and after, such as records, feedback or the view of a person who knew the learner then
4.3Review which explanations and routines from LO1 to LO3 the learner will keep, and state the next step and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own setbacks, is defined. The test at 4.2 is non-routine because the evidence may not support the claim. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.2. Review effectiveness: 3.3 and 4.3.

Boundary. The learner recovers from their own setbacks. Supporting the resilience of a team or of other people is outside this unit. ZHF-CO-03 is about acting before the outcome is known. ZFF-CH-03 is about forecasting and going through a change. This unit is about explaining and recovering from a setback, so the units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A setback record with its sort (LO1), ratings and written sessions (LO2), a routine log (3.2) and an evidence check with a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale 1978; Seligman 1990; Maier and Seligman 2016; Seligman and Schulman 1986; Pennebaker and Beall 1986; Kross et al. 2014; Spera, Buhrfeind and Pennebaker 1994; Sonnentag and Fritz 2007; Crum, Salovey and Achor 2013; Coan, Schaefer and Davidson 2006; Tedeschi and Calhoun 1996; Frazier et al. 2009; Seery, Holman and Silver 2010; Masten 2001; Bonanno 2004. Checked 21 October 2026.

Care Fluency
ZHF-CA-03

Caring for Others and Accepting Care

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyCareCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to give care where it is needed, without losing themselves, and to accept it. Learners predict how much a small kindness will mean, give it and ask. They identify who around them needs support and what kind, and give it. They find where caring costs them too much and try a way of caring that protects their energy. They then ask for help they would normally avoid asking for, and compare.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how caring they seem. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge kindness or warmth. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 4.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction. The learner chooses the people and the help involved, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private or taking on a caring duty. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare a prediction of how much a small kindness will mean with how it was received.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select a small kindness to give a person in own work or life, such as a written thank-you, and record in writing a prediction of how much it will mean to them
1.2Give it, then ask the person how it felt to receive, and record the answer
1.3Compare the answer with the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the difference, with reference to research on how givers judge kindness
LO2
The learner will: Be able to identify who needs care and what kind, and give it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify people in own work or life who may need support, and whether each needs emotional, practical, information or feedback support
2.2Give one person practical support matched to their need, without drawing attention to it, and record what was done
2.3Describe how the person responded, and judge whether the support matched the need
LO3
The learner will: Be able to care for others without losing themselves.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe the difference between feeling a person's distress and acting with compassion, using an example from own life
3.2Identify signs in own week that caring for others is costing the learner too much
3.3Select and use one way of caring that protects own energy, and review its effect
LO4
The learner will: Be able to accept care from others.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify one piece of help the learner would normally avoid asking for, and record in writing a prediction of how the person asked will respond
4.2Ask for the help, and record what happened
4.3Compare what happened with the prediction made at 4.1, and review what it shows about own habits of asking

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, care given and received in own work and life, is defined. The acts at 1.2 and 4.2 are non-routine because the other person's response is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 1.2 and 2.3. Review effectiveness: 3.3 and 4.3.

Boundary. The learner gives and accepts care in their own work and life. Building a culture of care in a team, or managing other people's wellbeing as a line manager, is outside this unit. ZFF-EI-03 reads and manages emotions. This unit acts on another person's need and on the learner's own, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A kindness forecast and answer (LO1), a support map and record (LO2), an energy record with a short review (LO3) and a request record (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Connection Fluency
ZHF-CN-03

Building the Connections a Life Needs

Level3TQT15 hoursCredits1.5GLH8 indicativeFluencyConnectionCriteria15

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to build the connections their own life needs, on purpose. Learners compare how much they think someone liked them after a conversation with what that person says. They map their connections by kind and find where the map is thin. They invest time in one connection of each kind and count the hours. They then repair one relationship after a rupture and review what changed.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how sociable they are. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge warmth, confidence or attitude. The wow moment sits at 1.3, where the learner's prediction of how much they were liked is set against the other person's own rating. Other people can be recorded by initials or by role. No criterion requires the learner to disclose anything private, and at 5.1 the learner chooses which rupture to work on and how much to say about it. Learners can always reach a person for support. The research on social ties and survival is taught as a research finding, and the unit makes no health claims.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare how much they think someone liked them after a conversation with what that person says.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record, straight after a conversation with someone new or little known, a prediction of how much that person liked the learner, on a stated scale
1.2Obtain the other person's own rating of the conversation on the same scale
1.3Compare the rating with the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on the liking gap
LO2
The learner will: Be able to map own connections by kind: close, friends, weak ties and bridges to other worlds.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Draw a map of own connections, sorting them into close ties, friends, weak ties and bridges to other worlds, and justify the placing of any connection that could fit more than one kind
2.2Describe what each kind of connection gives the learner, with one example of each from own life
2.3Record conversations with weak ties over one week, and compare days with more of them against days with fewer
LO3
The learner will: Be able to identify which kinds of connection each part of own life needs, and where own map is thin.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify the main parts of own life, such as work, home or a goal, and the kinds of connection each needs
3.2Identify where own map is thin against those needs, giving reasons
3.3Name one bridge to a world the learner wants to enter, and describe how a person already in that world is likely to see the learner's approach
LO4
The learner will: Be able to invest in one connection of each kind, on purpose.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Select one connection of each kind to invest in, justify each choice against the thin areas found at 3.2, and estimate the hours each needs, with reference to research on the time friendship takes
4.2Choose how and when to give the hours to each connection, such as in person or by call, explain the choice, and keep a record of each contact over an agreed period
4.3Compare the hours given with the hours planned at 4.2, and explain the difference
LO5
The learner will: Be able to repair a relationship after a rupture.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Describe a rupture in a relationship in own life that has not yet been repaired, including what has been put off
5.2Carry out one act of repair, recording what was done and how the other person responded
5.3Review how well own investment at LO4 and repair at 5.2 worked, and state the next step, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

5 learning outcomes, 15 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, the learner's own connections, is defined. The repair at 5.2 is non-routine because the other person's response is not known in advance, and the hours at 4.2 depend on other people's time. Identify, select and use: 2.1, 3.2, 4.1 and 4.2, where the learner places connections, picks which to invest in and chooses how, and gives reasons. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 4.3. Aware of different perspectives: 1.3 and 3.3. Review effectiveness: 5.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 2.1 now asks the learner to justify borderline placings, 4.1 ties each choice to the gaps found at 3.2, and 4.2 replaces scheduling with a reasoned choice of how and when to give the hours.

Boundary. The learner builds their own connections. Helping other people build theirs, or building connections across a team or organisation, is addressed at Level 5 and is outside this unit. ZHF-CF-03 works on a conflict that keeps returning. This unit repairs one rupture, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A liking-gap record (1.1, 1.2), a connection map (2.1, 3.2), a weak-ties log (2.3), an hours plan and contact record (4.1, 4.2), a repair record (5.2) and a short review (5.3), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

ZHF-CF-03

Stepping Out of Conflict

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyConnectionCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to step out of a conflict that keeps coming back in their own life. Learners map one recurring conflict and find each role they have played in it. They write the other person's reason in words that person would sign. They retell the conflict as an outsider would see it. They then open a hard conversation without blame, predicting the response first, and review what changed.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not whether they are a calm or reasonable person. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge attitude or temperament. The wow moments sit at 3.3, where the outsider's account is set against the learner's own, and 4.2, where the other person's response is set against the learner's prediction. The drama triangle and its ways out are taught as practitioner models, not tested findings, and the unit says so. The learner chooses which conflict to work on and should choose one where a conversation is safe. A conflict that involves harm or risk is not suitable for this unit. Other people can be recorded by initials or by role. No criterion requires the learner to disclose anything private. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to map one recurring conflict in own life and find each role they have played in it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe one conflict in own work or life that keeps returning, including what it is about and how often it has returned
1.2Map one recent round of the conflict onto the roles of persecutor, rescuer and victim, marking the moment the learner moved into each role
1.3Judge whether the conflict comes from a lasting difference to be managed or a problem that can be solved, giving reasons
LO2
The learner will: Be able to recognise when self or others take one of the roles.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify two occasions over an agreed period when the learner took one of the roles, describing what was said or done
2.2Identify one occasion when another person took one of the roles, describing the switch that followed
2.3Write the other person's reason for the last round of the conflict, in words that person would sign, and explain how it differs from the reason the learner had assumed
LO3
The learner will: Be able to step out of a conflict role as creator, challenger or coach.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Write an account of the latest round of the conflict as a neutral third party would see it
3.2Select the way out that matches the role identified at 2.1, and describe what it would look like in this conflict
3.3Compare the account at 3.1 with the learner's own map at 1.2, and explain the difference with reference to research on self-distancing
LO4
The learner will: Be able to say the hard thing clearly, without blame.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Write the first two sentences of a hard conversation, check them against the features of conversational receptiveness, and record a prediction of how the other person will respond
4.2Hold the conversation, recording what was said, and compare the other person's response with the prediction made at 4.1
4.3Review how well stepping out of the role and the new opening worked, and state the next step, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one recurring conflict the learner is part of, is defined. The conversation at 4.2 is non-routine because the other person's response is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 2.3. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner works on a conflict they are part of. Mediating other people's conflicts, or handling conflict in a team the learner leads, is addressed at Level 5 and is outside this unit. ZHF-CN-03 repairs one rupture in a relationship. This unit works on a conflict that keeps returning and the roles inside it, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A conflict map (1.1, 1.2), a role log (2.1, 2.2), the other person's reason (2.3), a third-party account (3.1), a conversation plan and record (4.1, 4.2) and a short review (4.3), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Karpman 1968; Gottman and Silver 1999; Pronin, Lin and Ross 2002; Waytz, Young and Ginges 2014; Emerald 2005; Grossmann and Kross 2014; Finkel et al. 2013; Carrère and Gottman 1999; Gottman et al. 1998; Yeomans et al. 2020; Rosenberg 1999. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-FB-03

Asking For and Using Feedback

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyConnectionCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to get feedback that helps and to use it. Learners ask some people for feedback and others for advice, predicting first which will be more useful. They name which trigger fired when they rejected a piece of feedback. They give one piece of feedback that is specific and kind. They then act on feedback, show the person what changed and review what worked.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how open they are to criticism. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge openness or attitude. The wow moment sits at 1.3, where the replies the learner received are set against their own prediction of which request would work better. The three triggers are taught as a practitioner model, not a tested finding. Other people can be recorded by initials or by role. No criterion requires the learner to disclose anything private, and at 2.1 the learner chooses which feedback to work on. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to ask for feedback that is useful.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select one piece of own work, and record a prediction of whether asking for feedback or asking for advice will produce more concrete, usable comments
1.2Ask at least four people for input on the work, asking half for feedback and half for advice, and keep the replies
1.3Compare the two sets of replies with the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on asking for advice
LO2
The learner will: Be able to name which trigger fired when they rejected feedback: truth, relationship or identity.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Describe a piece of feedback the learner rejected or found hard to take, including what was said and the situation it was said in
2.2Identify which trigger fired, truth, relationship or identity, giving reasons
2.3Restate the point the feedback made, apart from who made it, and evaluate which parts of it were accurate
LO3
The learner will: Be able to give feedback that is specific and kind.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify a situation where the learner held back feedback, and describe it from the other person's point of view, using the question "if I were them, would I want to know?"
3.2Give one piece of feedback that says where the person is going, how they are doing and where next, and that is about the task rather than the person
3.3Record how the feedback was received, including anything the person did with it, and interpret what the response shows about how well the feedback was framed
LO4
The learner will: Be able to act on feedback and show the change.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Select one piece of feedback received during the unit, and make a change in own work in response, keeping a record of what was changed
4.2Tell the person who gave the feedback what was changed, and ask them for advice on the next step
4.3Review how well asking for, receiving and acting on feedback worked across the unit, and state the next step, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, feedback on the learner's own work, is defined. The requests at 1.2 and 4.2 and the feedback given at 3.2 are non-routine because the replies are not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 1.1, 2.2 and 4.1, where the learner picks the work, the trigger and the feedback to act on, and gives reasons. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 3.1. Review effectiveness: 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 3.3 now asks the learner to interpret the response to their feedback, not only record it.

Boundary. The learner asks for, uses and gives feedback in their own work and life. Running appraisals, managing other people's performance or designing feedback processes for a team is addressed at Level 5 and is outside this unit. Feedback given at 3.2 is to a colleague, friend or family member, not as their manager.

Evidence

A request log with the prediction and replies (1.1, 1.2), a trigger record (2.1, 2.2, 2.3), a feedback record (3.2, 3.3), a change record (4.1, 4.2) and a short review (4.3), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Ashford and Cummings 1983; Blunden, Kristal, Whillans, Yoon, Burd, Bremner and Yeomans 2026; Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer 2015; Kluger and DeNisi 1996; Cohen and Sherman 2014; Stone and Heen 2014; Hattie and Timperley 2007; Abi-Esber, Abel, Schroeder and Gino 2022; Yeager et al. 2014; Walker and Smither 1999; Smither, London and Reilly 2005; Finkelstein and Fishbach 2012. ZHF-TM-03

Making a Team Work

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyConnectionCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to make a team they belong to work better, as a member. Learners predict how safe other members feel to speak up, then ask them anonymously and compare. They act in ways that make it safer for others to speak. Before a decision, they contribute what only they know and propose that others do the same. They then estimate their own share of the work, compare the team's claimed shares and review what worked.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does as a team member, not whether they are a good team player. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge attitude or likeability. The wow moments sit at 1.3, where the team's anonymous answers are set against the learner's prediction, and 4.2, where the team's claimed shares are set against the learner's own estimate. Answers at 1.2 stay anonymous and optional. The learner proposes the question and agrees it with the other members before it is used. Other people can be recorded by initials or by role. No criterion requires the learner to disclose anything private.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare own view of how safe a team feels to speak up with the views other members choose to share.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select a team the learner belongs to as a member and holds no authority in, and describe own position in it, including status relative to others
1.2Record a prediction of how safe other members feel to speak up, then propose one short anonymous question to the other members, agree with them whether and how it is used, and record the answers they choose to give
1.3Compare the answers with the prediction made at 1.2, and explain the difference with reference to research on status and psychological safety
LO2
The learner will: Be able to act in ways that make it safer for others in the team to speak up.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Describe one unwritten rule in the team about when speaking up is risky, and how it looks to a member with less status than the learner
2.2Carry out two actions that invite others to speak, such as asking a quieter member's view, recording what happened
2.3Raise one problem or mistake in own work with the team, and record how others responded
LO3
The learner will: Be able to contribute to a shared decision as a member, and agree roles with the other members.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Before a piece of shared work, contribute one thing only the learner knows that bears on it, suggest that the others each do the same, and record what was shared
3.2Propose who might decide what and who might do what, agree a split with the others, and explain where the agreed split differs from the proposal
3.3Evaluate whether what was shared at 3.1 changed the decision, giving reasons
LO4
The learner will: Be able to share the work and the credit.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Estimate own share of one piece of team work as a percentage, after listing what each other member did
4.2Ask each other member to estimate their own share, add the shares, and compare the total and the learner's estimate with 100 percent
4.3Review how well own actions at LO2 to LO4 worked for the team, and state the next step, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one team the learner belongs to, is defined. It is non-routine because the answers at 1.2 and 4.2, the responses at 2.3 and the agreed split at 3.2 are not in the learner's control. Identify, select and use: 1.1, 2.2 and 3.2, where the learner picks the team, the actions and a proposal to put to the others. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 3.2, 3.3 and 4.2. Aware of different perspectives: 2.1, and 3.2, where the learner explains how the others' views changed the proposal. Review effectiveness: 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: LO1 and LO3 were recast so the learner proposes, contributes, asks and agrees as a member, and never runs the survey or the meeting, and 3.2 now asks the learner to explain how the agreement differed from their proposal.

Boundary. The learner acts as a member of a team, never as its leader. They propose, contribute, ask and agree with others. They do not direct other members, assign them work, decide for them or run the team's meetings or processes, and they hold no authority over the others. Leading a team, including setting its direction, running its processes as its manager or being accountable for its members, is addressed at Level 5 and is outside this unit. A learner who manages a team uses a team they belong to as a member, such as a project or peer group, so the evidence stays at this level.

Evidence

A safety prediction and anonymous results (1.2), an unwritten-rules note (2.1), an actions log (2.2, 2.3), a meeting record (3.1, 3.2), a credit tally (4.1, 4.2) and a short review (4.3), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Checked 21 October 2026.

Mind, Body and Spirit Fluency
ZHF-MB-03

Thinking With the Whole Self

Level3TQT15 hoursCredits1.5GLH8 indicativeFluencyMind, Body and SpiritCriteria15

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to notice how their mind, body and sense of meaning shape their own thinking. Learners predict how often their mind wanders, then sample it for a week and compare. They catch body signals before a feeling has a name. They test one change to sleep, movement or time outdoors on their own thinking. They practise a habit of stillness or awe, and name what gives their life meaning, from any faith or none.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how calm, well or spiritual they are. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge wellbeing, belief or attitude. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own records are set against their own prediction. The unit makes no health claims. It teaches what research found about attention and thinking, and the test at LO3 measures thinking, not health. No criterion asks for a change to diet, medication or treatment. Meaning is approached from any faith or none, and no criterion asks the learner to state a faith or belief. No criterion requires the learner to disclose anything private. Learners can always reach a person for support.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to track where own mind is and how they feel, several times a day for a week.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record a prediction of how often own mind wanders from what the learner is doing in a typical day, as a percentage
1.2Sample several times a day for a week what the learner is doing, whether the mind is on it, and own mood on a stated scale
1.3Chart the samples, compare the result with the prediction made at 1.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on mind-wandering
LO2
The learner will: Be able to notice what own body signals before own mind names the feeling.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Record three occasions when a body signal, such as tension or a change in breathing, was noticed before the feeling had a name
2.2Interpret what each signal may have been responding to, with reference to research on body signals and decisions
2.3Describe one decision that noticing a signal earlier changed, or could have changed
LO3
The learner will: Be able to test how sleep, movement or time outdoors changes own thinking.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select one change to sleep, movement or time outdoors and one measure of own thinking, and record a prediction of the effect
3.2Run the test for two weeks, recording the change and the measure each day, including days missed
3.3Compare the result with the prediction made at 3.1, and evaluate what a test on one person can and cannot show
LO4
The learner will: Be able to practise a habit of stillness or awe and record its effect.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Choose between at least two habits of stillness or awe, such as a weekly awe walk, explain why the chosen habit suits own routine, and plan when it will take place
4.2Carry out the habit over an agreed period, recording each occasion and what was noticed, and interpret any pattern across the occasions
4.3Review how well the habit worked, using the records at 4.2, and state whether to continue, change or stop it and when that will be checked
LO5
The learner will: Be able to identify what gives own life meaning, from any faith or none.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Identify the sources of meaning in own life, drawing on any faith or none, and select the one that matters most, giving reasons. The learner chooses what to name and may describe it in general terms
5.2Distinguish between meaning the learner already has and meaning they are still searching for, using a measure from research that scores the two separately, and interpret what own result shows
5.3Compare own main source of meaning with that of a person who finds meaning differently, from any faith or none, and evaluate what the learner takes from the difference

5 learning outcomes, 15 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, the learner's own attention, body signals and habits, is defined. The test at LO3 and the habit at 4.2 are non-routine because their results are not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1, where the learner chooses the change, the habit and the main source of meaning, and gives reasons. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.2, 3.3, 4.2, 5.2 and 5.3. Aware of different perspectives: 5.3. Review effectiveness: 3.3 and 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 4.1, 4.2 and 5.1 to 5.3 now ask the learner to choose, interpret or evaluate in place of selecting a single habit, keeping a log and describing meaning.

Boundary. The learner works on their own thinking and their own life. Supporting other people's wellbeing, or shaping the wellbeing of a team or organisation, is addressed at Level 5 and is outside this unit. The unit gives no health, medical or therapeutic advice.

Evidence

A mind-wandering prediction and sample chart (1.1, 1.2, 1.3), a body-signal log (2.1), a two-week test record (3.1, 3.2), a habit log and review (4.2, 4.3) and a meaning statement (LO5), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Thinking Fluency
ZHF-CT-03

Testing Claims and Own Reasoning

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyThinkingCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to test their own reasoning as hard as they test other people's. Learners review an argument of their own as if a stranger had written it, predicting first how well it will hold up. They check a claim by reading other sources about it, not by reading it more closely. They identify common reasoning errors in their own thinking. They then state a judgement on mixed evidence as a probability, and review it later against what happened.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not whether they are a good thinker. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge open-mindedness or attitude. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 4.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to find in own reasoning an error of a kind that is easy to spot in someone else's.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe an argument made by someone else that contains a reasoning error, and name the error
1.2Select an argument the learner made in the past about a decision in own work or life, and record a prediction of how well it will hold up when reviewed
1.3Review the argument at 1.2 as if a stranger had written it, and compare what is found with the prediction, with reference to research on the bias blind spot
LO2
The learner will: Be able to test a claim against its evidence.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select a claim met in own work, the news or an AI answer, and state what evidence would show it to be false
2.2Check the claim by reading laterally, recording at least two independent sources consulted outside the original
2.3Judge whether the claim holds, giving reasons drawn from the sources at 2.2
LO3
The learner will: Be able to identify common reasoning errors in own thinking and in others'.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify two common reasoning errors, such as judging by how easily examples come to mind, in examples from own work or life
3.2Describe an occasion when own view on a topic affected how the learner read the evidence about it
3.3Describe how a person with the opposite view would read the same evidence, and where the two readings differ
LO4
The learner will: Be able to reach and explain a judgement when the evidence is mixed.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Set out the evidence for and against a question from own work or life where the evidence is mixed
4.2State a judgement on the question as a probability, naming what new evidence would change it
4.3Review the judgement after an agreed period against what happened or what new evidence showed, and state what to change in own reasoning next time

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, testing own arguments and the claims the learner meets, is defined. The judgement at LO4 is non-routine because the evidence does not settle it. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 4.2. Aware of different perspectives: 3.3. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner tests their own reasoning and the claims they meet. Teaching others to reason, or setting how a team weighs evidence, is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above. ZFF-AI-03 assesses checking the output of AI tools on tasks in own role. This unit is about the learner's own arguments and claims from any source, so the two assess different evidence. Where 2.1 uses an AI answer, the same evidence may not also be counted for ZFF-AI-03.

Evidence

A reasoning review with its prediction (LO1), a claim check log (LO2), an error log (LO3) and a probability judgement with its later review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Avianca, SDNY 2023; Tversky and Kahneman 1974; Kahneman 2011; Pennycook and Rand 2019; Kahan, Peters, Dawson and Slovic 2017; Lord, Ross and Lepper 1979; Mellers et al. 2014; Hauenstein et al. 2025; Tetlock 2005. ZHF-QU-03

Finding the Right Question

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyThinkingCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to decide what the problem is before solving it. Learners write several versions of a real problem before choosing one. They run a timed burst of questions on a problem they have already solved, predicting first whether it was the right one. They question an AI answer until its weakest claim shows. They then reframe a problem by asking what could be taken away, and review whether the new question worked better.

Design note. The unit assesses the questions the learner writes and what they do with them, not curiosity. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge whether the learner is inquisitive. The wow moments sit at 2.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction or rating.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to find the problem in a real situation before solving it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe a problem from own work or life as it was first presented, and the solution first thought of
1.2Write at least three different statements of what the problem might be, before choosing a solution
1.3Select one statement of the problem and explain why it was chosen over the first version
LO2
The learner will: Be able to generate and sort questions on a real problem.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select a problem the learner has already solved, and record a prediction of whether it was the right problem to solve
2.2Generate questions on the problem in a timed burst, recording every question asked without answering any
2.3Sort the questions by how far each changes the problem, mark any that suggest the wrong problem was solved, and compare the result with the prediction at 2.1
LO3
The learner will: Be able to question an AI answer until its weakest claim shows.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Put a question from own work or life to an AI tool, and record its answer and own rating of how far the answer can be trusted
3.2Ask follow-up questions that test the answer's claims against sources outside the tool, recording each question and what it showed
3.3Identify the weakest claim in the answer, explain why it is the weakest, and compare the finding with the rating at 3.1
LO4
The learner will: Be able to reframe a problem when the question is wrong.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify a problem in own work or life where the first question led to adding something, and describe a solution that takes something away instead
4.2Describe how another person affected by the problem would frame it differently
4.3Review whether the reframed question led to a better result than the first, and state the question the learner will ask first next time

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, a real problem from own work or life, is defined. The question burst at LO2 is non-routine because the learner does not know in advance whether the problem will change. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.2. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner finds and reframes problems in their own work and life. Leading a team or a meeting to define a problem is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above. ZFF-AI-03 assesses whether AI output is fit for a task in own role. LO3 here is assessed on the questions the learner asks, not on the task. ZHF-CT-03 tests a claim against its evidence. This unit assesses the questions that decide what the problem is, so the units assess different evidence and the same record may not be counted for more than one.

Evidence

A problem statement log (LO1), a question burst record with its prediction (LO2), an AI questioning record (LO3) and a reframing review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi 1976; Abdulla et al. 2020; Wedell-Wedellsborg 2017; Quote Investigator 2014; Graesser and Person 1994; Gregersen 2018; Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino 1977; Dell'Acqua et al. 2023; Mata v. Avianca, SDNY 2023; Duncker 1945; Adams et al. 2021. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-LN-03

Learning How to Learn With AI

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyThinkingCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to study in the ways that work, not the ways that feel like they work. Learners compare rereading with self-testing on their own material, predicting first which will last a week. They plan their own learning with spaced sessions and self-tests. They set an AI tool to quiz them instead of giving answers. They then review what worked for them and change how they learn.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how motivated they are. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge commitment or attitude. The wow moment sits at 1.3, where the learner's own score a week later is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare rereading with self-testing on own material, a week later.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select two comparable sets of material the learner needs for own work or life, and study one by rereading and the other by self-testing
1.2Record, straight after study, a prediction of how much of each set will be remembered a week later
1.3Test own recall of both sets a week later, and compare the scores with the prediction at 1.2, with reference to research on testing and confidence
LO2
The learner will: Be able to plan own learning with spaced practice and self-testing.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify something the learner needs to remember, and the date by which it must be remembered
2.2Choose between two spacing schedules for the material at 2.1, such as even gaps or gaps that grow longer, and produce a study plan with self-tests on the one chosen, explaining the choice against the date at 2.1
2.3Carry out the plan, recording before each self-test a judgement of how well the material is known and the score achieved, and adjust the next gap where the score shows the material was forgotten or already secure
LO3
The learner will: Be able to use AI to test oneself, not to skip the thinking.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select a written rule for an AI tool that quizzes the learner on own study material, such as how many tries come before it may give the answer or what kind of hint it may give, and explain why that rule suits the material
3.2Keep a record of the quiz sessions, including the questions missed, and interpret the pattern in what was missed to decide what to restudy and how
3.3Compare a session under the rule at 3.1 with a session where the tool gave answers, and explain the difference in what was remembered afterwards
LO4
The learner will: Be able to review what worked and adjust own learning.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe how another person, such as a colleague or family member, studies, and compare their method with the evidence in own records
4.2Review the plan at LO2 against the judgements and scores recorded at 2.3, stating which methods worked best and how accurate own judgements were
4.3State the change to be made to own way of learning, when it will start and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, the learner's own study of their own material, is defined. The comparison at LO1 is non-routine because its result is not known in advance and often contradicts the learner's belief, and the gaps at 2.3 change with scores the learner cannot predict. Identify, select and use: 1.1, 2.2 and 3.1, where the learner chooses a schedule or a quiz rule and gives the reason. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3, 3.2 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.1. Review effectiveness: 4.2 and 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 2.2, 2.3, 3.1 and 3.2 were set procedures and now each require a choice between options or a reading of the learner's own scores, with the scope kept to the learner's own study.

Boundary. The learner changes how they themselves learn. Designing learning for other people, or setting how a team learns, is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above. ZFF-GM-03 plans and carries out a piece of learning to keep a skill current in own role. This unit is about the method of study and the learner's judgement of their own memory, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A study comparison with its prediction and scores (LO1), a spaced study plan and session log (LO2), an AI quiz record (LO3) and a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Roediger and Karpicke 2006; Dunlosky et al. 2013; Karpicke and Blunt 2011; Ebbinghaus 1885; Cepeda et al. 2008; Kornell and Bjork 2008; Bjork 1994; Bastani et al. 2025; Nelson and Dunlosky 1991; Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell 2013. Checked 21 October 2026.

Creative Fluency
ZHF-CR-03

Making Original Work With AI as a Partner

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyCreativeCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to get past the first ideas, theirs and the machine's. Learners keep generating ideas past the point where they expect to run dry, predicting first how many more will come. They move a solution from an unrelated field into their own brief. They use AI to widen the options while keeping their own direction. They then make something, share it with people who make similar work and improve it from the response.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner produces and records, not whether they are a creative person. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge flair or attitude. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 4.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction or rating.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to push past own first ideas on a real brief.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select a real brief from own work or life, and record a prediction of how many more ideas the learner could produce once the first ideas run out
1.2Generate ideas on the brief past the point where they first seem to run dry, recording them in order
1.3Compare the later ideas with the earlier ones, stating which are more original and why, and compare the count with the prediction at 1.1
LO2
The learner will: Be able to combine ideas from fields unrelated to the brief.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify a solution used in a field unrelated to the brief
2.2Apply the solution to the brief to produce at least one new option, describing what was moved and what was changed
2.3Evaluate the combined option against options from within the brief's own field
LO3
The learner will: Be able to use AI to widen the options without letting it set the direction.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Record in writing own direction for the work before asking an AI tool for ideas
3.2Use an AI tool to generate options, including asking it to work step by step or from different starting points, and record its output
3.3Compare the AI's options with own options and with the direction at 3.1, identifying where the tool pulled the work towards the common answer
LO4
The learner will: Be able to make something, share it and improve it from the response.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Produce a finished piece of work from the brief, and record own rating of how it will be received
4.2Share the work with at least two people who make similar work, recording their responses
4.3Revise the work in response, and review how own rating at 4.1 compared with the responses

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one real piece of own work, is defined. Generating past the first ideas at LO1 and combining fields at LO2 are non-routine because the outcome is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.2. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner makes original work of their own. Running creative sessions for a team, or setting a team's creative direction, is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above. Sharing work with peers at 4.2 is part of the learner's own process, not leading others. ZHF-TA-03 judges and cuts options, including options AI has made. This unit makes the work, so the two units assess different evidence and the same AI output may not be counted for both.

Evidence

An ideas log with its prediction (LO1), a combination record (LO2), an AI options record set against the written direction (LO3) and the finished work with responses and revision (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

ZHF-TA-03

Judging Quality and Saying Why

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyCreativeCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to judge quality and give reasons that hold. Learners look at their own work from a year ago, predicting first how it will look now. They rank work by comparing it in pairs, then rank it again later to see whether their reasons hold. They separate what they like from what works for an audience. They then ask AI for many options and cut them down, saying why each one went.

Design note. The unit assesses the learner's judgements and the reasons they record, not whether they have good taste. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to share or judge the learner's preferences. The wow moment sits at 1.3, where what the learner now sees in their own old work is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to name what they now see in own work from a year ago that they could not see then.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select a piece of own work from at least a year ago, and record a prediction of how it will look now
1.2Identify at least three faults or features in the work that the learner did not see at the time, and name each one
1.3Compare what is found with the prediction at 1.1, and explain the gap between what the learner can now see and what they could then make, with reference to research on perceptual learning
LO2
The learner will: Be able to rank work and explain the choice.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Rank a set of at least six comparable pieces of work by comparing them in pairs
2.2Write a reason for each choice at the time it is made
2.3Rank the set again after an agreed interval without sight of the first ranking, and explain any differences between the two rankings and their reasons
LO3
The learner will: Be able to separate "I like it" from "it works for this audience".
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe a piece of work the learner likes, and identify how much of the liking comes from having seen it, or work like it, before
3.2Identify the audience the work is for, and state what it needs to do for them
3.3Describe how a member of that audience judges the work, using their own words where possible, and where their judgement differs from the learner's
LO4
The learner will: Be able to choose and cut from options AI has made.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Use an AI tool to produce at least twenty options for a real piece of own work
4.2Cut the options to three, writing one line on why each rejected option was cut
4.3Review the final choice after it has been used, stating whether it worked and what the learner would cut differently next time

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, judging own work and work the learner chooses between, is defined. The second ranking at 2.3 is non-routine because the learner cannot know in advance whether their reasons will hold. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 4.2. Aware of different perspectives: 3.3. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner judges quality in their own work and in the choices they make. Judging other people's work as their manager, or setting quality standards for a team, is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above. ZHF-CR-03 makes original work. This unit judges and cuts, so the two units assess different evidence and the same AI output may not be counted for both.

Evidence

A year-on review with its prediction (LO1), two paired rankings with written reasons (LO2), an audience comparison (LO3) and a cut list with its later review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Checked 21 October 2026.
