Story Fluency
ZHF-ST-03

Explaining and Telling Stories People Remember

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyStoryCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to explain what they know so that other people follow it and remember it. Learners tap out a song for someone, predicting first whether it will be named, and link the result to their own unclear explanations. They turn a point into a story with a person, a problem and a change. They speak to a group and check a day later what stuck. They then shape one message for three audiences and test each one.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner prepares, delivers and records, not how confident a speaker they are. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge charisma or polish. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to find where own expertise makes them unclear to others.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record a prediction of whether a listener will name a well-known song the learner taps out, then tap it out for a friend or colleague and record the result
1.2Describe an occasion when own explanation of a topic from own work or life was unclear to someone who knew less about it
1.3Compare the result at 1.1 with the prediction, and explain how the same gap affected the explanation at 1.2, with reference to research on the curse of knowledge
LO2
The learner will: Be able to turn a point into a story with a person, a problem and a change.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select a point from own work or life that needs to be explained to someone
2.2Write the point as a short story with a named person, a problem and a change
2.3Test the story and a plain statement of the point on another person, and record which one changed their view more
LO3
The learner will: Be able to speak to a group and check what they remember a day later.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Prepare a short talk for a group the learner already speaks to, with a single clear point, a story and a concrete example, and record a prediction of what the group will remember
3.2Deliver the talk to the group, adapting it in response to how the group reacts, and record the change made, the signal that prompted it and why that change was chosen, or, where no change was made, the signal that showed the point was landing
3.3Check a day later what members of the group remember, and compare it with the prediction at 3.1
LO4
The learner will: Be able to shape one message for three different audiences.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Write three versions of one message for three named audiences, stating what each audience needs
4.2Test each version on a real person from that audience, recording their response
4.3Review which version worked best for each audience, and which version the learner now recalls as the facts, with reference to research on saying is believing

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, explaining a point from own work or life, is defined. Delivery at 3.2 and the recall check at 3.3 are non-routine because how a group reacts, and what it remembers, is not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2, where the learner reads the group and chooses a change during delivery. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3, 3.2 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.1 and 4.2. Review effectiveness: 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 3.2 was a set procedure, delivering the talk, and now requires the learner to adapt it to the group's reaction and justify the change.

Boundary. The learner explains their own knowledge and tells their own stories. Speaking to a group at LO3 is part of the learner's own communication, not leading it. Coaching others to communicate, or setting the messages a team or organisation uses, is outside this unit and sits at Level 5 and above.

Evidence

A tapping record with its prediction and an unclear-explanation account (LO1), a story with its test record (LO2), talk notes with the prediction and day-later recall check (LO3) and three versions with their test responses and review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

ZHF-IN-03

Persuading and Negotiating Fairly

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyStoryCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to make a case and reach an agreement without pressure or tricks. Learners test how well they understand a view they hold strongly by explaining how it would work. They make a case to a real person who disagrees, framed in that person's values. They negotiate on interests rather than positions, predicting first what the other side wants. They then write the strongest case against their own view and say what they now accept.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not whether they win. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge confidence, charm or attitude, and no criterion rewards getting an outcome at the other person's cost. The learner chooses the view used at LO1, and no criterion requires a political or private view to be disclosed. Conversations are evidenced by the learner's own notes; no recording of the other person is required. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to explain how a strongly held view of their own would work in practice, and test their certainty in it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Select a view the learner holds strongly, and record a rating of their certainty in it and of their understanding of how it would work
1.2Explain in writing, step by step, how the view would work in practice, marking each point where the learner was unsure
1.3Rate certainty and understanding again, compare the ratings with those at 1.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on the illusion of explanatory depth
LO2
The learner will: Be able to make a case to someone who disagrees.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify a real person in own work or life who disagrees with the learner on a matter, and describe the values that matter most to that person
2.2Prepare a case framed in that person's values rather than own, using no tactic the learner would object to if it were used on them
2.3Make the case in conversation, record how the other person responded, and evaluate which parts of the case moved them and which did not
LO3
The learner will: Be able to negotiate on interests rather than positions.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe a real negotiation in own work or life, the position each side holds, and a written prediction of what the other side wants
3.2Use questions to find the other side's interests, and record what those interests turned out to be
3.3Compare the interests found at 3.2 with the prediction at 3.1, and describe an option that meets interests on both sides
LO4
The learner will: Be able to change own mind when the other side is right.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Write the strongest case against the view used at LO1
4.2State which part of the case against own view the learner now accepts, and the evidence that brought the change
4.3Review how own way of persuading and negotiating has changed across the unit, and state the next step and when it will be taken

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one view and one negotiation from own life, is defined. The conversations at 2.3 and 3.2 are non-routine because the other person's response is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 2.1 and 4.1. Review effectiveness: 4.3.

Boundary. The learner persuades and negotiates in their own conversations, for themselves. Negotiating on behalf of a team or an organisation, or leading other people to change their views, is above Level 3 and outside this unit.

Evidence

A certainty record (1.1, 1.3), a written explanation (1.2), conversation notes (2.3), a negotiation record (3.1 to 3.3) and a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Rozenblit and Keil 2002; Fernbach et al. 2013; Sloman and Fernbach 2017; Cialdini 1984; Feinberg and Willer 2015; Broockman and Kalla 2016; Fisher and Ury 1981; Thompson and Hrebec 1996; Galinsky et al. 2008; Follett 1925; Lord, Lepper and Preston 1984; Tetlock and Gardner 2015. Checked 21 October 2026.

Freedom Fluency
ZHF-FD-03

Keeping Own Attention and Options

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyFreedomCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to keep control of their own attention and widen their own choices at work. Learners predict how much of their phone use is started by notifications, then log a day and find out. They set rules that change the situation in advance and track whether the rules hold. They decide which of their own tasks to hand to AI and which to keep practising. They then take a first step to build a skill that would travel to another employer.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how disciplined they feel. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge willpower or attitude. The pick-up log records who started each pick-up, not what was looked at. The wow moment sits at 1.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to find out what starts own phone use, and take back time from it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record a prediction of what share of own phone pick-ups in one day will be started by a notification
1.2Log each phone pick-up across one day, recording whether it was started by a notification or by the learner, and identify the times and apps where pick-ups cluster
1.3Compare the log with the prediction at 1.1, explain the difference, and select three pick-ups to remove
LO2
The learner will: Be able to set and keep rules for own attention.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select at least three rules for own attention that change the situation in advance, such as notification settings or where the phone is kept, and explain how each targets a pattern found at 1.2 or a pick-up chosen at 1.3
2.2Keep a record over two weeks of how often each rule held, including when it was broken and why, and interpret the pattern in when and why rules broke
2.3Review which rules worked, with reference to research on self-control, and change or drop the ones that did not
LO3
The learner will: Be able to decide which of own tasks to hand to AI and which to keep.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify tasks in own work that an AI tool could do or help with, and select the three where the choice to hand over or keep matters most to own work, giving the reason for each
3.2Judge for each task whether to hand it over, share it or keep it, giving reasons that include the skill the learner would lose by not practising it
3.3Describe how a colleague or someone in a similar role decides the same question differently
LO4
The learner will: Be able to widen own options at work with skills that travel.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify which of own skills would be valued by other employers and which only by the current one
4.2Select one transferable skill or one contact outside own close circle to develop, take a first step, and record what happened
4.3Review how own attention and options have changed across the unit, and state the next step and when it will be taken

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own attention and own options, is defined. The rules at LO2 are non-routine because the learner chooses them from their own log and whether they hold is not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.2. Interpret and evaluate: 1.2, 1.3, 2.2 and 3.2. Aware of different perspectives: 3.3. Review effectiveness: 2.3 and 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 were logging and rule-keeping procedures and now require the learner to find the pattern in their own log, choose rules that target it, and interpret why rules broke; 3.1 was a list and now requires the learner to select the tasks where the choice matters most and give reasons.

Boundary. The learner manages their own attention and their own tasks. Setting attention or AI rules for a team is above Level 3 and outside this unit. ZFF-AI-03 assesses using and checking AI tools on work tasks. LO3 here assesses the choice of which tasks to keep practising, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A pick-up log (1.1 to 1.3), a rules record (2.1, 2.2), a task judgement (3.1, 3.2), a skills record (4.1, 4.2) and a short review (2.3, 4.3), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Simon 1971; Heitmayer and Lahlou 2021; Kushlev, Proulx and Dunn 2016; Mischel, Shoda and Rodriguez 1989; Watts, Duncan and Quan 2018; Duckworth, Gendler and Gross 2016; Allcott et al. 2020; Bainbridge 1983; Dell'Acqua et al. 2023; BEA 2012; Becker 1964; Deming 2017; Rajkumar et al. 2022; Granovetter 1973. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-MD-03

Handling Social Media and Outrage

Level3TQT15 hoursCredits1.5GLH8 indicativeFluencyFreedomCriteria15

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to use social media on their own terms. Learners predict how their feeds will affect their mood, then log a week and compare. They pause before acting on posts that provoke them. They check a widely shared claim before sharing it, recording what they believed first. They disagree online without joining a pile-on. They then change their own feed so it serves a goal they have set.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not which views they hold. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge attitude, and no criterion requires a political view to be disclosed: the learner chooses the posts and claims used. Evidence describes posts without naming any private individual. Pile-ons and outrage can be upsetting, so learners can always reach a person for support, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to track how own feelings change across a week of feeds, and what caused each change.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record, before the week starts, a prediction of how own feeds will affect own mood and which kinds of post will move it most
1.2Keep a log across seven days of each marked change in own feeling while using feeds, with the post or source that caused it
1.3Compare the log with the prediction at 1.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on what spreads online
LO2
The learner will: Be able to notice own emotional reaction to a post before acting on it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify from the log at 1.2 the kinds of post that most often prompt an urge to share, reply or react
2.2Use a pause before acting on at least five posts that prompt a strong reaction, recording the feeling named and the action then taken
2.3Describe how the actions taken after the pause differed from what the learner would have done without it
LO3
The learner will: Be able to check a viral claim before sharing it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select a widely shared claim the learner has seen, and record whether they believe it before checking
3.2Check the claim by leaving the page to find out who is behind it and what other sources say, recording each step
3.3Judge whether the claim is accurate, misleading or false, and compare the judgement with the belief recorded at 3.1
LO4
The learner will: Be able to disagree online without joining a pile-on.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe a real online pile-on from public posts, including what started it and how it grew
4.2Describe how the person targeted and an onlooker might each have seen the pile-on
4.3Write a reply that disagrees with a view by addressing the point rather than the person, and explain why it does not add to a pile-on
LO5
The learner will: Be able to shape own feed so it serves own goals.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Identify the follows, subscriptions and settings that most shape what appears in own feed
5.2Make at least three changes to own feed so it serves a goal the learner has stated, recording each change
5.3Review after an agreed period how the changes affected own feed and own goal, and state the next step

5 learning outcomes, 15 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own feeds over a set period, is defined. The check at LO3 is non-routine because its result is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 4.2. Review effectiveness: 5.3.

Boundary. The learner manages their own feeds and their own posts. Moderating content for others, or setting social media policy for a team or an organisation, is above Level 3 and outside this unit.

Evidence

A feed log (1.1 to 1.3), a pause record (2.2), a claim check (3.1 to 3.3), a pile-on description and reply (LO4) and a feed review (LO5), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Kramer, Guillory and Hancock 2014; Rathje, Van Bavel and van der Linden 2021; Allcott et al. 2020; Brady et al. 2017; Crockett 2017; Brady et al. 2021; Martel, Pennycook and Rand 2020; Vosoughi, Roy and Aral 2018; Wineburg and McGrew 2019; Pennycook et al. 2021; Sawaoka and Monin 2018; Ronson 2015; Bakshy, Messing and Adamic 2015; Guess et al. 2023; Bagchi et al. 2024; Milli et al. 2025. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-MO-03

Managing Money in a Changing Working Life

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyFreedomCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner money skills for a working life that keeps changing. Learners read a payslip and work out what minimum payments on a debt really cost. They estimate their hourly pay, then calculate their real hourly pay and compare. They set a savings goal with a default step that does not rely on willpower. They then compare ways to grow their income, including new skills.

Design note. The unit teaches money skills and guidance only. It never gives personal financial advice, and no criterion asks for or rewards a personal recommendation. For free, impartial guidance, learners are pointed to MoneyHelper, run by the Money and Pensions Service. The assessor judges the method, not the learner's financial choices. Learners may use rounded figures or a sample payslip, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private. Every criterion asks for a description, a record, a calculation or an action. The wow moment sits at 2.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own estimate.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to interpret pay, tax, pensions and debt in the UK, and find impartial guidance.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Interpret a payslip, own or a sample, identifying the gross pay, income tax, National Insurance, pension contribution and net pay, and explain how one change, such as a pay rise or a higher pension contribution, would alter the net pay
1.2Calculate, using a worked example, the time to clear and the total cost of a credit card balance under the minimum payment and under a fixed higher payment the learner selects, and interpret what the difference shows about paying only the minimum; the learner may use own figures instead if they choose
1.3Identify a money question the learner has, compare at least two sources of information on it, and evaluate which is free, impartial and reliable, such as MoneyHelper, giving reasons
LO2
The learner will: Be able to work out own real hourly pay, and price purchases in hours of own working life.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Record an estimate of own hourly pay from headline pay and contracted hours
2.2Calculate own real hourly pay by taking off work costs and counting all the hours work takes, such as travel
2.3Compare the result at 2.2 with the estimate at 2.1, explain the difference, and price three planned purchases in hours of own working life
LO3
The learner will: Be able to set a savings goal and a plan to reach it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Set a savings goal with an amount, a date and a reason
3.2Plan a default step that moves money towards the goal without a decision each month, and state whether it was put in place
3.3Review progress against the plan after an agreed period, and adjust the plan
LO4
The learner will: Be able to compare ways to grow own income, including new skills.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify at least three ways own income could grow, such as a pay rise, a change of employer or a new skill, and select which are open to the learner now, giving the reason for each
4.2Evaluate the likely gain, cost and time of each, using sourced figures and the real hourly pay from 2.2
4.3Describe how a person at a different stage of working life might weigh the same options, and select own next step

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own pay, saving and income, is defined. The effect of a change at 1.1 and the income options at 4.2 are non-routine because the figures depend on the learner's own situation. Identify, select and use: 1.2, 1.3, 3.2, 4.1 and 4.3. Interpret and evaluate: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.3 and 4.2. Aware of different perspectives: 4.3. Review effectiveness: 3.3. The sources compared at 1.3 are judged for impartiality, never for a personal recommendation, and the assessor judges the method, not the learner's choices. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: the LO1 stem was "Know" and its criteria were reading, a given sum and finding a source, close to Level 2; LO1 now asks the learner to interpret a payslip change, interpret a repayment comparison and evaluate sources of guidance, with no personal financial advice. 1.2 keeps the worked example, and the learner may use own figures only if they choose. 4.1 was a list and now requires the learner to select which income routes are open to them, with reasons.

Boundary. The learner manages their own money. Giving money guidance to other people, or any personal recommendation on a financial product, is outside this unit; personal recommendations are regulated advice under FCA rules.

Evidence

A payslip and debt worksheet (LO1), an hourly pay calculation (2.1 to 2.3), a savings plan and review (LO3) and an income comparison (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Lusardi and Mitchell 2014; Fernandes, Lynch and Netemeyer 2014; Kaiser et al. 2022; Stewart 2009; FCA Occasional Paper 42; Robin and Dominguez 1992; DeVoe and House 2012; Whillans et al. 2017; Madrian and Shea 2001; Thaler and Benartzi 2004; DWP, Workplace pension participation and savings trends 2009 to 2021; Hershfield et al. 2011; Money and Pensions Service 2020; Mincer 1974; Resolution Foundation 2019; Mani et al. 2013. Checked 21 October 2026.

Responsibility Fluency
ZHF-RS-03

Making and Keeping Commitments

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyResponsibilityCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to spend their energy on what they can change, and to keep the commitments they make. Learners log a week of worries, predict which will come true, and find out. They make three commitments, predict how long each will take, and track them daily. They own a real mistake and take a step to repair it. They then choose how to respond in a situation under pressure.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how they feel about themselves. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge confidence, guilt or attitude. The learner chooses which worries and which mistake to use. Learners can always reach a person for support, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 2.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to sort own worries by what can be changed, and track what happens to them.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Record own worries across one week, sorting each into what the learner can change and what they cannot
1.2Predict for each worry whether it will come true, and record what happened at the end of an agreed period
1.3Compare what happened with the predictions at 1.2, and explain what the result shows about where own energy went
LO2
The learner will: Be able to make, track and keep commitments.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Select three commitments for one week from the things the learner can change at 1.1, giving the reason for each choice, write down a predicted time for each, and tell one person
2.2Log progress on each commitment every day of the week, and where the log shows a commitment slipping, choose a change to the approach and record it
2.3Compare the time each commitment took with the prediction at 2.1, and explain the difference with reference to research on the planning fallacy
LO3
The learner will: Be able to own a mistake and repair it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Describe a real mistake in own work or life, and what it affected
3.2Describe how a person affected by the mistake saw it
3.3Take an action to repair the mistake, and record what was done and how it was received
LO4
The learner will: Be able to choose a response under pressure.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify a situation under pressure that is coming up, and interpret the response the learner usually chooses, including what sets it off and what it costs
4.2Select a technique from the unit that suits the situation at 4.1, such as naming the feeling or calling nerves excitement, giving the reason for choosing it over another, use it in that situation, and record what happened
4.3Review how well the logs and techniques in this unit worked for the learner, and state the next step and when it will be taken

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, own worries and own commitments over a set period, is defined. The repair at 3.3 and the response at 4.2 are non-routine because how each will be received or will play out is not known in advance. Identify, select and use: 2.1, 2.2 and 4.2, where the learner chooses commitments, a change of approach or a technique and gives the reason. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3, 2.3 and 4.1. Aware of different perspectives: 3.2. Review effectiveness: 4.3. Levelling pass 21 October 2026: 2.1, 2.2, 4.1 and 4.2 were set procedures, making, logging, describing and using, and now each require a choice with a reason or a reading of the learner's own pattern.

Boundary. The learner makes and keeps their own commitments and repairs their own mistakes. Holding other people to account, or managing the commitments of a team, is above Level 3 and outside this unit.

Evidence

A worry log (LO1), a commitment log (2.1 to 2.3), a repair record (LO3) and a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Rotter 1966; LaFreniere and Newman 2020; Borkovec et al. 1983; Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994; Harkin et al. 2016; Tangney, Stuewig and Mashek 2007; Breines and Chen 2012; Kachalia et al. 2010; Gross 1998; Gross and John 2003; Lieberman et al. 2007; Brooks 2014. Checked 21 October 2026.

ZHF-ET-03

Making and Owning Ethical Decisions

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyResponsibilityCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to notice a moral choice and make it with care. Learners name the values at stake in a real dilemma from their own work or life. They test a moral judgement they hold firmly, recording first how well they expect to justify it. They make a real decision and explain it to someone whose view they do not know. They then decide which of their own decisions should never be handed to a machine.

Design note. The unit assesses how the learner reaches and explains a decision, not which decision or view they hold. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge character or attitude. The learner chooses the dilemma and the judgement used, and no criterion requires disclosing anything private. The wow moment sits at 2.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to name the values at stake in a real dilemma.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe a real dilemma in own work or life, including the moment the learner first saw it as a moral question
1.2Identify the values at stake, such as care, fairness, loyalty or authority, and which of them pull against each other
1.3Describe how another person could weigh the same values differently and reach a different view
LO2
The learner will: Be able to test a moral judgement held firmly, and decide what to do with it.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify a moral judgement the learner holds firmly, and record how confident they are that they can justify it
2.2Write out the reasons for the judgement and test each one, recording which reasons hold
2.3Compare the result at 2.2 with the confidence recorded at 2.1, and decide whether to keep, revise or hold the judgement more lightly, giving reasons
LO3
The learner will: Be able to make and explain an ethical decision.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select a real decision facing the learner, describing the options and the people each option would affect
3.2Explain the chosen option step by step to a person whose view on it is not known in advance, and record the challenges they raised
3.3Review how the decision turned out against the reasons given at 3.2
LO4
The learner will: Be able to decide which of own decisions should not be handed to a machine.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1List decisions in own work or life that an AI tool could make or shape
4.2Judge which of those decisions should stay with a person, giving reasons that refer to the values at stake
4.3Compare the judgement at 4.2 with research on how people view machines making moral decisions, and state whether any choice changes

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one dilemma and one decision from own life, is defined. The dilemma is non-routine because the values in it pull against each other and no rule settles it. Interpret and evaluate: 2.3, 4.2 and 4.3. Aware of different perspectives: 1.3 and 3.2. Review effectiveness: 3.3.

Boundary. The learner makes and owns their own decisions. Setting ethical standards or policy for a team or an organisation is above Level 3 and outside this unit. ZFF-GV-03 assesses working within the rules for AI use at work. LO4 here assesses the learner's own judgement on which of their decisions should stay with a person, not what workplace rules allow, so the two units assess different evidence. Where the two differ, the learner follows workplace rules and may record the difference.

Evidence

A dilemma record (LO1), a judgement test (2.1 to 2.3), a decision record and review (LO3) and a machine decisions list (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Rest 1986; Graham, Haidt and Nosek 2009; Gioia 1992; Haidt 2001; Royzman, Kim and Leeman 2015; Lerner and Tetlock 1999; Fernbach, Rogers, Fox and Sloman 2013; Huang, Greene and Bazerman 2019; Weizenbaum 1976; Bigman and Gray 2018; Awad et al. 2018. Checked 21 October 2026.

The bridge to Future Fluency
ZFF-CH-03

Facing Change in Own Working Life

Level3TQT12 hoursCredits1.2GLH6 indicativeFluencyThe bridge to FutureCriteria12

Unit aim

This unit gives the learner the skills to go through a change in their own working life with a clear view of it. Learners compare how they expected a past change to feel with how it turned out. They map which tasks in their work will stay and which will change. They run one small experiment with a new way of working, predicting the result first. They then review what has ended, what has started and what comes next.

Design note. The unit assesses what the learner records and does, not how they feel about change. Every criterion asks for a description, a record or an action. No criterion asks an assessor to judge confidence or attitude. The wow moments sit at 1.3 and 3.3, where the learner's own evidence is set against their own prediction.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to compare how a past change in own working life was expected to feel with how it turned out.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Describe a past change in own working life that was expected to be difficult, including how long the difficulty was expected to last
1.2Describe how the change turned out, using evidence such as dates, messages or records from the time
1.3Explain the difference between what was expected and what happened, with reference to research on how people forecast their own feelings
LO2
The learner will: Be able to map which tasks in own work are likely to stay, change or go.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1List the tasks that make up own role in a typical week, with the time each takes
2.2Judge whether each task is likely to stay, change or go as technology changes, giving reasons
2.3Describe how a person affected by the same change sees it differently from the learner
LO3
The learner will: Be able to run a small, safe experiment with a new way of working.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Select one new way of working to test, and record in writing a prediction of how it will go
3.2Carry out the experiment over an agreed period, keeping a record of what happens, including setbacks
3.3Compare the result with the prediction made at 3.1, and explain the difference
LO4
The learner will: Be able to review own transition through a change and set the next step.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Describe what has ended in own work as a result of the change, and what has started
4.2Review how well own predictions at 1.1 and 3.1 matched what happened, and what that shows about own forecasting
4.3State the next step to be taken, when it will be taken and how progress will be checked

4 learning outcomes, 12 assessment criteria.

Level check

Well defined but may be complex and non-routine: the brief, one change in own working life, is defined. The experiment at LO3 is non-routine because its result is not known in advance. Interpret and evaluate: 1.3 and 3.3. Aware of different perspectives: 2.3. Review effectiveness: LO4.

Boundary. The learner goes through a change in their own working life. Leading other people through change is Change Fluency at Level 6 (ZFF-CH-06). ZFF-GM-03 develops a new skill for changing tasks. This unit is about how the learner forecasts and goes through the change itself, so the two units assess different evidence.

Evidence

A forecast log (1.1, 3.1), a task map (2.1, 2.2), an experiment record (3.2) and a short review (LO4), each captured in learn.zavmo.ai as an xAPI statement against the criterion it meets.

Research behind the unit

Gilbert et al. 1998; Wilson and Gilbert 2005; Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson 2013; Autor, Levy and Murnane 2003; Eloundou et al. 2024; Bessen 2015; Weick 1984; Ibarra 2003; Bandura 1977; Bridges 1980, 1991; Amabile and Kramer 2011. Checked 21 October 2026.

Section 4

What we know is not yet right

Listed plainly, so that a reviewer has this list before finding any of it.

1

No assessor has read these units. They are written to the descriptor and re-levelled by reviewers who did not write them. Nobody with assessment experience has read them yet.

2

Two units are borderline at Level 3. ZHF-TM-03, because asking team members a question could read as running a survey. ZHF-MB-03, because naming sources of meaning sits close to private disclosure. Criterion 5.1 now lets the learner stay general. An assessor should read both first.

3

Credits are not whole numbers. 12 and 15 hours give 1.2 and 1.5 credits. Either the units are sized at 10 or 20 hours, or they are bundled into Awards whose totals round cleanly. To settle with the awarding organisation.

4

The gate is uneven in size. ZFF-GM-03 is 50 hours and ZFF-EI-03 is 15. A Human Fluency learner should not meet a 50-hour gate before a 12-hour unit. A short Growth Mindset unit may be needed.

5

Two overlaps need watching. ZFF-EI-03 and ZHF-RS-03 draw on the same emotion-regulation research, and ZHF-CN-03 and ZHF-CF-03 both deal with repair. Each boundary says one piece of evidence cannot count for both.

6

The safeguarding route does not exist yet. Units touching personal life assume a learner can always reach a person. That has to be in place before launch.

7

Sources are checked, not read in full. Research was checked twice against abstracts and records. The headline findings still need reading in full before submission.
